# GRUB boot artifacts

This directory pins the eight GRUB boot artifacts the disk and ISO builders consume, so a developer build needs neither a GRUB toolchain nor Docker. GRUB cannot be built on macOS, which is how a Docker container came to own these bytes; pinning the generated artifacts, with their provenance recorded, keeps the container out of every build and every suite. `manifest.txt` records the container digest, the archive state, each package version with its `.deb` SHA-256, the tool version, the module lists, the two embedded configurations' digests, and each artifact's size and SHA-256.

Six artifacts are for BIOS `i386-pc` boot of an MBR disk or an ISO:

* `bios-boot.img`: GRUB's MBR boot sector template. The embedder (`tools/image/grubembed.c`) copies its first 440 bytes into a disk's MBR, preserving the disk identifier and partition table.
* `disk-core.img`: the disk core image, with the embedded configuration `tools/image/grub-embed.cfg` and the modules to find and read the FAT boot partition and start a Multiboot kernel. The configuration searches for label `RACH2BOOT` and opens `/boot/grub/grub.cfg`; if that call returns, it searches for `RACH2RECOV` and opens `/boot/grub/recovery.cfg`. The disk modules are `biosdisk part_msdos fat normal multiboot configfile loadenv echo test serial terminal search search_label search_fs_uuid search_fs_file`. The embedder writes the core into the post-MBR gap.
* `disk-core-a.img` and `disk-core-b.img`: the same core prefixed with a serial marker (`GRUBCORE=A`, `GRUBCORE=B`). The GRUB replacement suites install them alternately and prove a swap by the marker the running core prints. `tools/image/mkgrubcore.sh` verifies and hands one out.
* `eltorito.img`: the El Torito boot image for ISOs, with the `iso9660` module, built in GRUB's `i386-pc-eltorito` output format.
* `boot-hybrid.img`: GRUB's hybrid MBR template, placed by `xorriso` so an ISO also boots when written to a USB device.

Two boot a GUID-partitioned disk, and the second boots an ISO or a stick by UEFI as well:

* `gpt-core.img`: the BIOS core for a GPT disk, with the embedded configuration of `disk-core.img` and the modules `biosdisk part_gpt part_msdos fat normal multiboot multiboot2 configfile loadenv echo test serial terminal search search_label search_fs_uuid search_fs_file`. The embedder writes it at the start of the disk's BIOS boot partition, since the sectors after the MBR hold the GUID table, and `bios-boot.img` in sector 0 loads it from there.
* `bootx64.efi`: GRUB's `x86_64-efi` image, from the package `grub-efi-amd64-bin`, which the disk builder installs as `\EFI\BOOT\BOOTX64.EFI` on the EFI system partition and the ISO builder in the ISO's EFI boot image. Its modules are `part_gpt part_msdos fat iso9660 normal multiboot multiboot2 configfile loadenv echo test serial terminal search search_label search_fs_uuid search_fs_file efi_gop efi_uga`, and its prefix is `/boot/grub` on the device the firmware loaded it from. Its embedded configuration, `tools/image/grub-efi-embed.cfg`, opens `$prefix/grub.cfg`, which is the boot partition's menu on a disk; if that call returns, it searches for `RACH2RECOV` and opens `/boot/grub/recovery.cfg`, as the BIOS core does.

The image is not signed, so a machine boots it only with Secure Boot turned off in its firmware.

`verify_grub.sh [ARTIFACT[=PATH] ...]` compares size and SHA-256 against the manifest; with no argument it checks every artifact beside the manifest, and `NAME=PATH` checks a copy at PATH against NAME's entry. Every consumer copies the artifacts it needs into its own working directory and verifies the copies, so the bytes checked are the bytes used and a modified file fails the build instead of reaching a disk. Every run also compares `tools/image/grub-embed.cfg` and `tools/image/grub-efi-embed.cfg` against the manifest's `embed-cfg` and `efi-embed-cfg` digests: the cores and the EFI image embed those files as they were at generation time, so editing one without regenerating fails the next build rather than shipping images whose configuration nobody checked.

## Regeneration

`regen_grub.sh` is a maintainer procedure and needs Docker; nothing in the ordinary build or the suites runs it. It points apt at one dated state of the Ubuntu snapshot archive (the `SNAPSHOT` identifier in the script; override with `RACH2_GRUB_SNAPSHOT` to move to newer packages), generates every artifact twice from clean directories in the pinned Ubuntu container, requires the rounds byte-identical, and rewrites the artifacts and manifest together. Regenerating is how a GRUB upgrade is chosen: the change is reviewed like any vendored-source update, and `tests/run grub`, `tests/run menu`, `tests/run install`, `tests/run sealed`, `tests/run drill`, `tests/run installer` and `tests/run uefi`, plus an ISO boot, must pass on the result before it lands.

This directory is the one exception to the source-first vendoring rule, recorded in `AGENTS.md`: the artifacts are generated output, pinned because the generating toolchain does not exist on every supported host. The manifest records the container digest and the snapshot identifier, which name the regeneration's inputs completely, along with every package the install added, the three GRUB packages' `.deb` digests, the tool version, the module lists, and the embedded configurations' digests. The one package that does not come from the snapshot is the `ca-certificates` bootstrap with what it pulls in, `openssl` among them, which carries trust anchors and no byte of an artifact; its versions are those of the container's default archive on the day, and the manifest records them as installed.
